At 7:40 on Tuesday, Lena Ortiz unlocked the rear workshop at Bell Street Printworks and began the scheduled ventilation check. The room held two screen-printing benches, a washout sink, and a small curing cabinet, with the extraction hood mounted above the ink table. The check was planned before the first production shift so the crew could use the room while the equipment was tested. Lena carried a calibrated vane meter, a smoke pencil, and the maintenance log from the office.

She first looked over the system without switching it on. A strip of blue tape on the hood marked the filter panel that had been opened the previous Friday. Its catches were seated, the gasket showed no tears, and no loose ink cloth had been left against the intake. Lena noted a light layer of paper dust on the ledge, but it had not reached the grille. She wiped the ledge and recorded the cleaning before moving to the fan isolator.

The fan started on the first attempt, though its sound was rougher than the steady hum recorded in the log two months earlier. Lena listened beside the motor housing and then at the duct bend above the drying rack. There was no repeated knock or scraping noise. A faint vibration came through the wall bracket, so she checked its two visible bolts with a spanner. Both were snug, and the bracket had no fresh marks where it met the wall.

At the hood, she held the vane meter in the center of each marked opening for a full minute. The readings varied slightly as the doors to the washout area moved, but settled when the room was still. She wrote down the average for the front, center, and rear positions rather than selecting the highest reading. The front position was the weakest. Lena repeated that measurement after checking that the meter's arrow faced into the airflow, and the second result was close to the first.

1. Hood and fan observations
   - Fan started normally and ran throughout the measurement period.
   - No obstruction was visible at the grille or in the accessible filter panel.
   - Airflow readings were recorded at three marked positions, with the front position lowest.
   - A small amount of vibration was felt at the wall bracket; its visible bolts were secure.

Lena next used the smoke pencil to see how air moved around the work surface. With the curing cabinet closed, the smoke traveled upward toward the hood from all three bench positions. At the front edge it drifted sideways before rising, which matched the lower meter reading. When the washout door stood open, a cross-draft pulled the smoke toward the corridor. Closing that door restored the upward path, so she entered the door position beside each set of observations.

The shop supervisor, Ben, came in while Lena was recording the second smoke test. He asked whether the fan had passed its check. Lena replied, “I’ve finished the measurements, but I haven’t compared them with the service limits yet.” Ben said the first shift was due in twenty minutes and moved the drying rack away from the hood. The rack had been parked closer than usual because a delivery pallet occupied its marked floor space.

Lena measured the distance from the rack to the hood and wrote it in the log, then repeated the center reading with the rack in its usual position. The value changed only slightly, while the smoke rose more cleanly from the rear bench. She photographed the original rack position and the clear working position with the shop tablet. The images showed the hood, floor marks, and rack wheels; no staff members were in the frame.

She also checked the make-up air grille near the entrance. Its face was clear, but a folded delivery sheet had been tucked under the lower edge of the grille cover. Lena removed the sheet and placed it with the paperwork on the supervisor’s desk. The grille cover remained secure, and she did not remove it because the check required only a visual inspection of its accessible face. The airflow at the hood was then measured once more with the corridor door shut.

Ben asked Lena to send the preliminary figures to the morning crew so they would know where to leave the rack. She said she would put the figures and the rack photograph in the maintenance log, but would not circulate the preliminary note to the crew until she had checked the service limits. The crew could still see the floor marks and keep the rack in its usual position. Ben acknowledged the distinction and returned to the press room.

Lena compared the readings with the limits printed on the equipment service sheet, using the range for the hood’s installed fan setting. She copied that range into her notes so a later reviewer could see which reference she had used. The front reading remained the lowest of the three, and the repeat measurements were consistent with the earlier set. She did not adjust the fan control or open the ductwork during this visit; those actions were outside the scheduled visual and airflow check.

Before leaving, she entered the time, instrument identification, room conditions, door positions, and rack location in the maintenance log. She attached the two photographs and filed the removed delivery sheet with the shop’s daily papers. The log showed the fan running, the repeated measurements, and the observed cross-draft when the washout door was open. At 8:32, Lena signed the entry and returned the meter to its case in the office cabinet.

This is the dye room log for the north window run on Tuesday the ninth of April. I am recording the work from the first inspection through the last rinse because the blue batch will be compared with the sample from March. The room was opened at six forty, and the wall thermometer read eighteen degrees. The night crew had left the exhaust fan running, and the floor was dry except beside the sink, where a narrow strip of cotton twill had been hung to drain. I moved it to the rack before bringing in the wool. The revised reading sheet should go to Leonie, not Emmett, because Leonie is keeping the comparison file and Emmett has the loom schedule.

Section one covers the incoming cloth. The wool came from roll W twenty seven and weighed twelve kilos six hundred grams after the paper wrapper was removed. The mill ticket listed a plain weave and a width of one hundred forty centimeters. There were two loose ends at the edge but no oil marks or visible stains. I cut the inspection strip from the marked end and wrote the roll number on its tag with the black laundry pencil. The cotton twill was a separate control cloth from bin C four, and it was not included in the wool weight. Both pieces were checked under the north window because the ceiling lamps make the dark yarn look warmer than it is in daylight.

The scour bath was prepared in the stainless tank with seventy liters of water at thirty eight degrees and a measured dose of neutral detergent. The wool stayed under the surface for twenty two minutes with slow movement by hand. I turned the folded center twice and kept the cloth away from the drain outlet. The first rinse ran clear after the third bucket, and the final rinse measured six point eight on the paper strip. There was no scent left from the detergent. I pressed water out with the wooden bar rather than twisting the fabric, then laid the wool flat on the mesh table for eleven minutes while the tank was emptied.

The dye recipe in the blue card calls for three hundred grams of indigo stock and forty five grams of the yellow modifier. For this run, I weighed three hundred grams of stock from bottle I twelve and used forty four point eight grams of modifier from jar Y six. The small difference is from the amount that stayed on the weighing paper, and I recorded the actual reading rather than rounding it. The water level was brought back to seventy liters before the stock was added. The assistant stirred for two full minutes with the broad paddle, then I checked that no clump remained at the bottom. The bath looked green under the room light and dark blue where it touched the side of the tank.

The wool entered at nine twelve and was worked slowly so the fold opened without pulling the selvage. I kept the timer beside the thermometer and turned the bundle at five minute intervals. The bath held between forty six and forty eight degrees for the first twenty minutes, then rose to forty nine when the heater cycled. The lid stayed partly open during that rise, and I reduced the setting by one mark. The cloth remained in the bath for thirty two minutes altogether. The exposed top edge showed a lighter band at removal, so I submerged that edge again for four minutes and noted the extra time on the log before lifting the whole piece.

The first rinse after dyeing was taken in a separate pail and came away blue green. The second rinse was less colored, and the third was nearly clear. I did not add soap at any stage after dyeing because the recipe card calls for water rinses only. The cloth was held over the tank until the drops slowed and then placed on the drying frame with the warp running parallel to the long side. The lower corner sagged about two centimeters, so I shifted the clips outward and checked that the edge was straight after the adjustment. The control strip went into the same rinse pails after the wool but was kept in its own labeled mesh sleeve.

At eleven thirty five, the wool was dry enough at the surface for a color reading, though the middle fold still felt cool. I used the handheld meter in three places and wrote down the values from the left edge, center, and right edge. The center was the darkest reading, and the right edge was slightly lighter. The difference was visible in daylight but not under the lamp. I did not describe the shade as a match because the March sample was not in the room today. The control strip measured more evenly across its width and showed a greener cast than the wool. I put both measurements in the margin so they can be compared when the earlier sample is brought back.

The drying frame was moved away from the radiator at noon after I noticed warm air reaching the bottom bar. The window remained closed because dust from the repair work in the hallway was still settling on the sill. The cloth stayed on the frame until two twenty and was then laid on clean brown paper with the tag facing up. I checked the selvage for dye transfer and found two small blue marks on the paper beneath the center fold. There was no mark beneath either end. I saved the marked sheet in the folder rather than discarding it and put a note beside the location of each stain so the next reading can be taken from an undisturbed part of the wool.

The final entry is for storage and handoff. The wool was rolled around a cardboard tube with the face side inward and tied at three points using the loose cotton tape from the worktable. The control strip was wrapped separately in clean tissue and placed in bin C four again. I wrote the batch date and roll number on both tags and left the dye card in the blue binder on the shelf. The temperature in the room at closing was nineteen degrees, and the fan was still running. The floor beside the sink had dried completely. I left the revised reading sheet on the desk in an envelope addressed to Leonie, not Emmett, and recorded that the March comparison sample remains outstanding.

The tournament will take place at the Alder Street Community Hall on May 18 and 19, with five rounds scheduled across the weekend. Organizers expect players from nearby counties as well as residents of the city, and the hall’s main room can hold 96 competitors. Registration closes on May 10, unless all places are filled earlier. The association has reserved a smaller room for analysis, quiet breaks, and parents accompanying junior players.

This year’s event is rated by the national chess federation and is open to players with current membership. A player whose membership has lapsed may renew through the federation before the first round, but the tournament desk cannot process renewals. The entry form asks for each player’s full name, federation identification number, rating, club if applicable, and a contact email address. Players without a federation rating may enter as unrated. Organizers have asked entrants to check their identification numbers carefully, since an incorrect number can attach a result to the wrong player’s record.

The registration page lists two sections. The Open Section has no rating ceiling, while the U1600 Section is limited to players rated below 1600 on the May rating list. Players may register for only one section. If an entrant’s rating changes before the list is published, the tournament director will use the published May rating to determine eligibility for U1600. I started the registration notes for the North Quay Open after the library committee asked me to check how the entry process worked for first-time players. The event was scheduled for October 12 and 13 at the Old Ferry Hall, and the organizers expected about 80 people. The hall had a main room with 12 tables, a smaller room beside the kitchen, and a narrow entrance where people would need to collect their badges. The tournament director was Mara Ellis, and the volunteer coordinating the check-in desk was Tomas Reed.

The first issue was that the registration page listed two different closing dates. The top of the page said entries would close on September 28, while the paragraph at the bottom said September 30. Mara told me the later date was correct because she had moved the deadline after the city extended the hall booking. She had not updated the first line yet, so I wrote down that the page needed one date, not that either date had been confirmed by the website team. The entry fee was 32 pounds for adults and 20 pounds for players under 18. The fee included lunch on both days but not accommodation. People could ask for a reduced fee by emailing the organizers, and the page said requests would be considered individually. It did not state an income threshold or promise that a request would be accepted.

Section One: Details to verify before opening the desk

1. The player list should show each entrant’s name, club if supplied, rating, and requested section.
2. The desk should have printed receipts for cash payments and a separate envelope for card terminal slips.
3. The organizers needed a clear process for a player whose payment appeared twice in the online account. Tomas said he had seen duplicate notices before but did not know whether both charges had actually settled.
4. The notices should explain that players had to tell the organizers about a withdrawal by email rather than assume a message in the tournament chat counted as formal notice.

I asked whether the chat could be used for quick questions, and Mara said, “It is fine for directions and arrival updates, but I still need the withdrawal in my inbox.”

The entry form asked for a full name, a contact email, a club when applicable, and a rating as of September 1. It also asked players to choose the Open or the Under 16 section. The Under 16 event required the player to be younger than 16 on the first day. There was no separate girls’ section and no junior prize listed outside that event. Mara said they would accept an unrated player but would ask for a short note about recent games so that the pairings could be checked. She did not say that an unrated player would be placed in a particular rating band. The form had a box for accessibility requests and a separate field for dietary needs; both were optional. The kitchen could provide vegetarian and dairy-free lunches, but Mara was still checking whether the caterer could handle a severe nut allergy.

I sat with Tomas at the hall one afternoon, and we walked through the route from the entrance to the desk. The first table was close to the door, but the queue could block the fire exit if it turned toward the coat hooks. The hall manager had asked them to keep a meter of clear space in front of that exit and had marked the area with blue tape. The smaller room could hold a waiting line, but it was also where the organizers planned to store clocks and spare sets. Tomas suggested putting the sign-in desk along the long wall and keeping one volunteer at the door to guide arrivals. No one had yet checked whether the tables would leave enough room for a wheelchair to pass between the registration area and the main playing room. The hall manager said they could move two tables if needed but asked for the final layout by the Monday before the tournament.

We also reviewed what players would receive after checking in. The packet was expected to include a name badge, a printed schedule, a hall map, and a small card with the tournament contact number. The schedule showed round one at 10:30 on Saturday and round five at 10 on Sunday, with later rounds listed as approximate times because the director wanted to allow for long games. Mara planned to post pairings on a board near the main room and on the event page. The page did not promise text alerts, and some participants had asked whether pairings would be available through an app. Tomas said they could not commit to that unless someone tested the software with the final player list. He had a spreadsheet from last year, but the old list included contact details and could not simply be shared with this year’s volunteers.

There were practical questions about arriving and paying as well. The nearest bus stop was on Quay Road, and the hall had a small car park that was shared with the library. After six o’clock, the library staff expected fewer visitors but had not reserved spaces for the tournament. One player had asked whether overnight parking was allowed, and Mara had referred the question to the hall manager rather than guessing. The organizers could take card payments through a handheld terminal or cash at the desk, but did not want volunteers to accept bank transfers into personal accounts. Tomas had drafted a cash count sheet with columns for the amount received, the receipt number, and the initials of the volunteer who counted it. Mara asked him to add a place to record a refund if one was issued before the entry deadline.

On Friday evening, the team planned to place signs from the Quay Road entrance to the hall door and check that the room was unlocked before setting up. They would bring extension leads, two spare clocks, a first aid kit, and paper copies of the contact list. The list was meant for the organizers and would include only the phone numbers volunteers needed during the event. The director wanted the public schedule to show when the desk opened and when late arrivals should contact a volunteer, but had not decided whether the desk would remain staffed through every round. I wrote down that we should not print the signs until the hall manager confirmed the route because the side entrance might be closed for maintenance on Saturday morning.

When I finished the notes, Mara asked me to send her the list of page changes and the unresolved questions. She said she wanted the deadline corrected first, then the allergy information checked with the caterer, and the room layout reviewed with the hall manager. She had not asked me to edit the public page, and I did not have access to its account.
